claims.text: A blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at the site path /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/, and it covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration from CDK to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure definitions to AWS (CDK is AWS-specific).
Debugging AWS CDK deployments was frustrating because of the CloudFormation templates it generates.
Multi-cloud infrastructure was nearly impossible with AWS CDK; AWS CDK supports AWS only.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster (faster deployments), more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience than AWS CDK.
Traditional infrastructure-as-code tools and approaches have often been geared more toward DevOps teams than application developers.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK).
AWS CDK allows developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.

With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code is essentially a code generator that produces an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) which is then executed to deploy resources, so the code the developer writes is not the code running during deployment.
The CDK/CloudFormation intermediary-format approach leads to difficulty debugging, lack of visibility into the deployment process, and challenges extending or customizing the deployment workflow.
A link to https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/comparisons/cloudformation/#what-is-aws-cloudformation exists and covers what AWS CloudFormation is.
The SST team expanded its focus beyond AWS to other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure, and found the AWS-centric nature of CDK and CloudFormation to be a limitation.
A link to https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/comparisons/aws-cdk/#what-is-aws-cdk exists and covers what AWS CDK is.
Pulumi supports multi-cloud deployment across AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging, whereas debugging with AWS CDK is hard because of CloudFormation.
Pulumi supports any programming language, whereas AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK deployments because Pulumi uses direct execution and CDK is slowed by CloudFormation.
Pulumi provides clear deployment state, whereas errors are hard to trace with AWS CDK.
Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows for extensibility, whereas AWS CDK extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management, whereas Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, whereas Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, instead of generating an intermediary format.
With Pulumi, the infrastructure code is the same code that runs during deployment, giving greater visibility into the deployment process and the ability to extend or customize it.
Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach lets SST's team easily work with a wide range of cloud and on-premises platforms.

SST's transition from CDK to Pulumi required re-implementing higher-level components built on CDK and handling edge cases and complex deployment scenarios, with the goal of matching and improving upon the previous version's functionality.

The Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights (https://www.pulumi.com/product/pulumi-insights/) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for infrastructure deployments.

Because Pulumi infrastructure code is the deployment code, the SST team could easily trace issues back to source, unlike the CDK/CloudFormation approach where CloudFormation templates obscure the underlying logic.

Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components, which the SST team used to integrate with cloud and on-premises services and implement complex deployment workflows.
With the CDK/CloudFormation approach, the SST team often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to achieve customization.
With Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach, the SST team was able to easily add support for new providers.
With SST built on Pulumi, users can manage all of their infrastructure (across multiple cloud providers and on-premises) through a single, consistent interface.
SST users can write their infrastructure logic in the same programming languages they use for their application code.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy it across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one consistent workflow.
The SST team is exploring deeper integration with application frameworks, expanded provider support, improved deployment workflows, and enhanced observability and monitoring, building on Pulumi.

Pulumi Cloud Deployments (https://www.pulumi.com/docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/) enables more advanced deployment workflows, such as faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, and more granular control over the deployment process.
Pulumi Insights provides better visibility into the deployment process and more robust monitoring and observability capabilities.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, as described in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand Pulumi workshop titled "Getting Stated with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" is available at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Pulumi offers upcoming Platform Engineering or DevOps workshops listed at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, in which constructs (components) are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST (Serverless Stack) makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console.
The SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
SST primarily relies on SaaS revenue through its managed platform and potentially supplemental income streams like enterprise services and consulting.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account (or Pulumi Cloud dependency); the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST stores deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account (self-hosted), not in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the framework.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework, from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.

With SST, infrastructure and application code are defined together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.
The SST team has repeatedly described their own architecture as built on the Pulumi engine since the v3 rewrite shipped.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs ("What is SST") say: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."
Independent developers who have compared SST, Terraform, and Pulumi directly describe the same architecture (SST built on the Pulumi engine).

Gautier Blandin, in "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis", writes: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
Kiryl Anoshka, in "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion", writes: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `platform/package.json` for SST's platform package lists as direct dependencies `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and the Pulumiverse `@pulumiverse/vercel` provider.
The SST repository is now at `anomalyco/sst` (formerly `sst/sst`) on GitHub.
`sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts`, resolves SST's own components, and those components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) translates each resource in Terraform-bridged providers into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine owns dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs underneath SST's CLI, component model, and local dev loop.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers, adapted for the Pulumi engine, instead of writing and maintaining their own.
Pulumi's engine can run without a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools in the same embedded way SST embeds the engine.
The Pulumi Terraform provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.

The internal link targets exist: /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/, /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/, /docs/iac/concepts/policy/, /docs/iac/concepts/components/, /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/.
Embedding the Pulumi engine gives SST a production-grade provisioning engine and hundreds of cloud providers without building either from scratch.

Nitric, a cloud-agnostic application framework, runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine; its own docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric deployment providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud and runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine; its Pulumi provider is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric, Defang, and SST each expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to their users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers; SST does not require a Pulumi account to work.
Most SST users never write any Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, resources that lack a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi inside an SST app and deployed as part of the same app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package has roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026, per the npm downloads API).
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub star count than SST itself (anomalyco/opencode, observed September 2026).
SST is still actively maintained and shipping, and the team's attention to opencode has not changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.

SST does not use Terraform directly: its components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine, SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI, and it does not write Terraform state.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides guardrails a platform team can enforce centrally, and Pulumi components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
An SST user is already running Pulumi's engine, and Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components can be used without leaving that same engine.

SST is a strong fit for an opinionated full-stack application framework, while Pulumi directly makes more sense when cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across applications is needed because SST does not expose those capabilities on its own.
The related post "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi" tells the fuller story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
